analysis.one_liner: Strips monopoly protections from brand-name drugs priced far above what other rich countries pay.
analysis.headline: Khanna's Prescription Drug Price Relief Act was introduced in the House with 4 cosponsors and referred to two committees, where no action has been taken since May 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the Department of Health and Human Services review every brand-name drug's price each year. Any drug priced above the median price charged in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan would be declared excessive, and the government would cancel the exclusivity that keeps generic competitors off the market — issuing open licenses so any company could make a cheaper version, with a royalty paid to the original maker. It also requires drug companies to disclose their pricing, research, and advertising spending, and creates a public database of the findings.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and insurers who pay U.S. brand-name drug prices that are higher than what the same drugs cost in other wealthy countries. Americans routinely pay several times the Canadian or German price for identical medicines. Generic and biosimilar makers would gain a new, legally protected path to sell cheaper versions, paying a reasonable royalty to the original developer. Taxpayers also benefit, since Medicare and Medicaid foot part of the bill for high U.S. drug prices.

how_it_helps.text: HHS must review all brand-name drugs at least annually and declare a price excessive if the U.S. average manufacturer price exceeds the median price in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan [S2][S3].

For a drug declared excessively priced, HHS must void the government-granted exclusivity that blocks generic competitors and grant open, non-exclusive licenses allowing anyone to make and sell the drug, with expedited 8-month review of generic and biosimilar applications [S3].
Licensed generic makers pay a reasonable royalty to the original patent holder and must sell below the excessive price, so developers are compensated while prices fall [S2][S3].

The bill requires manufacturers to report detailed pricing, research, and advertising spending for each brand-name drug and creates a public database of excessive-price determinations, with civil penalties up to 1% of a drug's gross revenues per day for noncompliance funding NIH research grants [S2][S3].
Any person can petition HHS for an excessive-price determination on a specific drug, and HHS must act within 90 days or publicly explain why not [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies, which would lose monopoly pricing power — and potentially large revenues — on any drug the government declares excessively priced. Some revenue would be recaptured through royalties, but generic competition generally cuts prices sharply. Companies would also bear new annual reporting costs.

drawbacks.text: The mechanism is aggressive: voiding exclusivity and issuing compulsory licenses whenever a U.S. price exceeds the median of five reference countries would override patents and regulatory exclusivities that Congress deliberately created to reward drug development, and companies could respond by launching new drugs abroad first or shifting investment [S3].

Comparing U.S. average manufacturer prices to foreign list prices is complicated by different rebate and pricing systems abroad, and a rigid median-price test could flag drugs whose U.S. net prices are actually lower after discounts [S3].

The bill leaves a great deal to the Secretary's discretion, including what counts as a reasonable royalty and how to weigh the factors in the fallback 'higher than reasonable' test, which could produce inconsistent or politicized determinations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the potential gains are large: U.S. prices for the same drugs are often multiples of prices in peer countries, and this bill attacks that gap directly rather than with negotiation. The tradeoff is real — it trades stronger patent protection for lower prices, which could modestly discourage some drug investment — but the royalty mechanism and the fallback test based on development costs and patient value acknowledge that tradeoff. It is a sweeping bill that would face serious implementation questions, but its costs fall on an industry with high margins, not on ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees, and neither has taken it up — no hearing, no vote, nothing since the May 2025 referral [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on May 21, 2025, joined by Rep. Jan Schakowsky, and it was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and in addition to the Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S3][S5].
No further action has been recorded — the bill has sat in committee since its referral [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers keep their current monopoly pricing and pay nothing, and the committees' leadership avoided a politically charged fight on their calendars.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican support is recorded, and the Republican-controlled committees have not moved the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill voids the exclusivities that keep generic rivals off the market whenever a drug's U.S. price exceeds peer-country medians, directly threatening monopoly revenues. Because the industry's gain comes from charging Americans more than other wealthy countries pay for the same drugs, its interest runs against patients'.

The bill grants open, non-exclusive licenses and 8-month expedited reviews, giving generic makers a fast legal route to sell cheaper versions. Their gain is the public's gain: lower prices for the same medicine.

analysis.trajectory: With only 4 cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action in months, the realistic path is that the bill sits in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress without a hearing or vote. Comparable international-reference-pricing and compulsory-licensing bills have repeatedly stalled in past Congresses.
